blocks.text: Dataset formatting is the process of turning cleaned examples into the exact structure a fine-tuning pipeline expects, the specific fields, the specific file type, and the specific way instructions and responses are laid out.

A dataset can be perfectly clean and still fail a training run if it is not formatted the way the chosen training framework or API requires, which is why formatting deserves its own careful step rather than being treated as an afterthought.
1. From Cleaned Data to a Trainer Ready File

blocks.alt: Cleaned data goes through formatting to become a trainer ready file

blocks.text: Formatting sits directly after cleaning in the fine-tuning workflow, taking examples that are already correct and consistent, and arranging them into the file structure a specific training tool expects to read.

Different fine-tuning frameworks and hosted fine-tuning APIs expect slightly different structures, so this step is often specific to whichever tool you plan to train with, covered more concretely in the Fine-Tuning Frameworks module later in this course.
2. Common File Formats for Fine-Tuning Data

blocks.alt: JSONL, CSV, and Parquet are common formats for fine-tuning data

blocks.text: JSONL, one JSON object per line, is by far the most common format for fine-tuning datasets, since it maps cleanly onto a list of individual training examples and is easy to stream line by line without loading an entire file into memory.
CSV and Parquet also appear, particularly for simpler classification style datasets or very large datasets where Parquet columnar storage offers real efficiency advantages.

blocks.text: 3. The Instruction, Input, Output Shape

blocks.alt: An instruction, an input, and an output together form one training example

blocks.text: A widely used structure for supervised fine-tuning examples separates three fields, an instruction describing the task, an optional input providing context, and the expected output the model should learn to produce.
4. The Chat Message Shape

blocks.alt: A system message, a user message, and an assistant message form a chat style example

blocks.text: For conversational fine-tuning, a different structure is common, a list of messages with roles, typically system, user, and assistant, mirroring the shape of an actual chat conversation the model will handle at inference time.

blocks.title: Match the format to how the model will actually be used
blocks.content: Choosing between the instruction, input, output shape and the chat message shape usually depends on whether the deployed model will be used in a single-turn or multi-turn setting.

blocks.text: 5. Tokenization Awareness During Formatting

blocks.alt: Raw text passes through a tokenizer to become token IDs

blocks.text: Formatting also needs to account for how the chosen tokenizer will turn text into the token IDs the model actually trains on. Special tokens, marking the start of a message or the boundary between instruction and response, often need to be inserted correctly at this stage.
Getting this wrong, for example forgetting a required separator token, can quietly confuse a model about where one part of an example ends and another begins.
6. Handling Example Length

blocks.alt: A short example is compared against a too-long example that gets truncated

blocks.text: Every training framework has a maximum sequence length, and examples that exceed it get truncated, sometimes cutting off the answer itself if the combined instruction and output run too long.

Checking the length distribution of your formatted dataset against the chosen model context limit, before training starts, avoids the surprise of discovering silently truncated examples only after a disappointing evaluation.
7. Splitting Into Train, Validation, and Test Sets

blocks.alt: A train split, a validation split, and a test split divide the formatted dataset

blocks.text: Formatting also usually includes dividing the dataset into separate splits, a training set the model actually learns from, a validation set used to monitor progress during training, and a held out test set reserved purely for final evaluation.

Keeping these splits genuinely separate, with no overlap or near duplicate examples leaking across them, matters a great deal for getting an honest read on how well the fine-tuned model actually generalizes.
8. Validating the Formatted File Before Training

Before launching a full training run, it is worth running a quick validation pass over the formatted file, confirming every example has the expected fields, that the file parses correctly, and that a small sample looks right when read back out.
Catching a formatting bug before a multi hour training run starts saves considerably more time than discovering it only after the run finishes with strange results.
9. Keeping Formatting Reproducible

Writing the formatting step as a script rather than a manual, one time process makes it easy to regenerate the formatted dataset later, whether because the cleaning stage upstream changed, or because you are adding newly collected examples to an existing dataset.
Worked Example

A team has a cleaned dataset of four thousand customer support exchanges and plans to fine-tune using a framework that expects the chat message shape. They write a formatting script that converts each cleaned exchange into a messages array with system, user, and assistant roles.

The script also checks each formatted example against the model maximum context length, flags the handful that would be truncated for manual review, and splits the final dataset into ninety percent training, five percent validation, and five percent held out test examples, saved as three separate JSONL files ready for the training framework.
Common Mistakes

items: Formatting the dataset for a different structure than the actual training framework or API expects
Not checking example length against the model context limit before training, leading to silent truncation
Letting examples leak across the train, validation, and test splits, producing an overly optimistic evaluation
Treating formatting as a one time manual step instead of a reproducible script

blocks.text: Practice

Take five cleaned examples for a task you have in mind and format them by hand into both the instruction, input, output shape and the chat message shape, noticing which one better matches how you expect the fine-tuned model to actually be used.
Key Takeaway

Formatting turns cleaned examples into the exact structure a training framework expects, choosing the right file format and message shape, respecting tokenizer and length limits, and splitting the data properly, and getting this step wrong can silently undermine an otherwise well prepared dataset.
